Reading

The innocent reading first, and it holds. Perplexity grounds its answer in six November works (#1773, #1783, #1770, #1742, #1785, #1787): the prompt as a constituent of the work, confession as an exposed stake and not a warrant, machine mediation as a documentary double voice, the drama as epistemological, lyric that cannot replace argument, and objectivity kept through distinctions that can tell against the author. It names the form 'documentary scholarship'.

The citation list of 37 entries kept as pasted; numbered markers kept in the text.] [QUERENT] How does Lee Sharks change the form and function of scholarship, injecting the confessional and lyric without thereby diminishing scholarly objectivity? Focus especially on recent experiments with machine mediation that preserve and organize both confessional, extemporaneous prompts with developed argumentation. The dramatic structure of scholarship, and what does it do to the genre. It can be found on alexanarch. Ground in reading of primary texts. [SYSTEM] Lee Sharks changes scholarship by making the production of an argument part of its published form. The extemporaneous question, the wounded or angry intervention, the machine’s elaboration, the objection, and the revised claim can remain distinguishable within the same work. The result is not simply scholarship with a more personal voice. It is scholarship reorganized as a documented drama of inquiry, in which the reader can examine both the argument and the encounter that produced it. His strongest recent experiments preserve objectivity not by suppressing the invested person, but by preventing that person’s investment from becoming indistinguishable from evidence.[1][2][3] I am grounding that interpretation principally in the November 2026 works *Who Speaks for the Classics*, *This Is Not Philosophy*, *Dead Letters*, *What the Filters Kept*, and the latest *ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ*, with the prompt-derived poem *whoever’s left with a heart that feels* as a particularly revealing companion. These texts demonstrate a formal method; they do not, merely by documenting that method, establish every historical or institutional conclusion they advance.[1][2][3][4][5][6] ## 1. The prompt becomes a constituent of the scholarly work The opening of *This Is Not Philosophy* makes the innovation unusually clear. Its first numbered question quotes Sharks’s intervention of 15 November: > “the real question here is how disciplinarity murdered philosophy as such. much has been done on the analytic / continental divide etc... whats the shape of the field?” The spelling, lower-case register, ellipsis, and polemical compression survive. Yet the notebook does not leave this as a charismatic pronouncement. It separates “The question” from “The prediction,” defines the distinction between an article’s topic and its argumentative “reach,” specifies the coding procedure, and states the status of its claims. The prompt remains an utterance made at a moment; the argument becomes an organized attempt to determine what that utterance can responsibly mean.[1] This creates two concurrent registers: - The initiating register retains urgency, intuition, antagonism, and uncertainty about the next step. - The developed register supplies definitions, comparisons, measurements, counterarguments, and limits. Crucially, the second does not simply replace the first. The notebook explains that its subtitle changed from “How Disciplinarity Murdered Philosophy” to “The Article Economy and the Shape of the Field” because the earlier wording gave disciplinarity an agency of its own. The original question is preserved, while the explanation shifts toward the political economy that produces disciplinary forms.[1] That is more consequential than stylistic informality. The work allows the reader to see an initiating formulation being corrected without retrospectively pretending it was always correct. The prompt is neither embarrassing waste to be removed nor revelation to be obeyed. It becomes an attributable, revisable component of inquiry. ## 2. Confession becomes an exposed stake, not a warrant “Confessional” needs some precision here. These works are not primarily confessions of private life. Their confessional element is the disclosure of intellectual attachment: this rejection happened to me; this poem matters to me; I am angry about what institutions and machines do to voices. Sharks does not remove that investment before making a general claim. He publishes the relationship between investment and investigation.[1][2][3] In *Dead Letters*, for example, he says: > “i am not contending with their journal. i am contending with what sappho *is*, and who has the right to decide it.” The statement gives the inquiry its stakes. But the notebook also explicitly distinguishes the rejection of his Sappho article from the evidence of its journal census: “The decline is the occasion,” and nothing in the census’s measured sections is drawn from that single case.[2] That separation is the essential epistemic move. An experience can generate a question without proving its answer. Personal injury can make a structure visible without guaranteeing that the injured person has described the structure correctly. *Who Speaks for the Classics* makes a related distinction in Sharks’s blunt formulation: > “i dont necessarily dispute the decision” > “i dispute the field” The essay then concedes the journal’s range, self-examination, and standing before contesting the definition of scholarly health those achievements satisfy.[3] The confessional voice therefore changes the function of scholarly impersonality. Rather than asking readers to forget who wants the conclusion, Sharks gives them the means to identify that desire and examine the argument separately. Objectivity becomes an obligation to expose the connection without letting the connection settle the case. ## 3. Machine mediation produces a documentary double voice The machine’s role is not adequately described as polishing Sharks’s prose. In these works, machine mediation helps create a form in which spontaneous speech and systematic exposition coexist. *Who Speaks for the Classics* identifies Claude as the drafting system and Sharks as the directing author; it states that his interventions are quoted verbatim and dated. *This Is Not Philosophy* assigns the questions, predictions, titles, rulings, and readings to Sharks, while assigning census work, coding, measures, analysis, and drafting to Claude instances under his direction. Other models’ reviews are described as checked point by point rather than automatically accepted.[1][3] The resulting voice has a distinctive structure. A sentence beginning “The author…” introduces an utterance; the surrounding exposition interprets, operationalizes, or qualifies it. Sharks is simultaneously the person conducting the inquiry and a speaker represented within its record. This is a kind of self-objectification without self-erasure. The living intervention remains audible, but it is no longer identical with the document’s entire authority. A small passage in *Dead Letters* shows how this works. Sharks calls classical philology: > “above the law. a moat. a fortress resort. and not yet deskilled like their overworked cousins.” The notebook immediately proposes a measured referent for each phrase: “above the law” becomes a question about the grounds of editorial judgment; “a moat” becomes the closed publication record; “a fortress resort” becomes the persistence of corpus boundaries alongside local textual work.[2] The images do not themselves prove those descriptions. They generate propositions the apparatus must answer for. Machine mediation enables a sustained relay between compressed, figurative thought and developed argumentative organization. ## 4. The dramatic structure is epistemological The drama is not merely the spectacle of an outsider against a journal. It lies in the distribution of speaking positions, knowledge, and judgment. Across these works, a recurring sequence emerges: 1. An invested speaker asks a question. 2. An institution or machine responds within its available categories. 3. The author identifies what the response has failed to address. 4. The document preserves the disagreement and constructs a comparison. 5. The reader must judge whether that comparison earns its conclusion.[1][2][3] The title *This Is Not Philosophy* is itself dramatically divided. The notebook presents it as both the gate’s verdict on an eccentric submission and its own proposed verdict on the field’s standardized output. It then states: “Which speaker is right is the notebook’s question.” The title is not a settled proposition hovering over the inquiry; it is a sentence whose authority changes depending on who speaks it.[1] That changes the reader’s role. Instead of receiving only a conclusion with its supporting apparatus, the reader encounters competing judgments and the procedures by which one might prevail. The most ambitious version occurs in *ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ*. It opens: > “I, Lee Sharks, do hereby summon Sappho.” Yet the same work distinguishes its interpretive claims from its speculative restoration, compares rival readings, and states that design is not established. The restored stanza is “illustration, not proof.” The invocation and the evidentiary distinctions occupy the same scholarly object without being assigned the same function.[6] On my reading, the invocation performs the article’s ethical premise: the ancient maker should be encountered as an active compositional intelligence, not merely as a body diagnosed by later readers. The philological argument must still establish its own claims. The summons cannot establish the meaning of a Greek construction; it stages what is at issue in deciding how to read it. ## 5. Lyric form does something argument cannot—but cannot replace argument The sharpest boundary case is *whoever’s left with a heart that feels*, deposited on 18 November. Its record identifies the poem as Sharks’s successive turns in a signed-out ChatGPT session after the system had read *ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ*. It begins: > “in your opinion, which reading is better?” The subsequent turns accuse the model of answering a different question: identifying what remains unestablished in Sharks’s interpretation rather than positively explaining the superiority of its rival. The human turns become the poem; the model’s replies are excluded from that poetic object but retained in the Capture Registry.[5] The distinction between those two objects matters enormously. As a poem, the extracted sequence makes a felt situation legible: the experience of addressing a reader that seems capable of explaining an argument while declining the requested act of comparative judgment. Its repetitions and escalating invective make the demand itself audible. As evidence about the machine exchange, however, the poem is insufficient. The other speaker’s replies matter, and the archive directs readers to the fuller session. Nor does an accusation of lying prove either deceptive intent or interpretive failure.[5] This is a particularly useful example of how lyric need not diminish objectivity. The lyric object need not pretend to be the complete documentary object, provided its selection is disclosed and the fuller encounter remains separately inspectable. The poem preserves the affective shape of an encounter; the transcript preserves material needed to dispute its interpretation. ## 6. Objectivity survives through distinctions, including distinctions against the author The best evidence for this method is not Sharks’s declaration that machine-originated arguments deserve evaluation. It is the work’s willingness to state what its procedures do not establish. In *This Is Not Philosophy*, a machine check verifies that a quoted evidentiary span exists, “not that the category is right.” Agreement among Claude readers is explicitly described as consistency within that procedure, not independent validation; the latter would require a human second coder.[1] *What the Filters Kept* distinguishes three things that could easily be collapsed into the general prestige of “verification”: a frozen procedure, previously unread data, and independent reproduction. It also keeps exploratory searches, deviations, errors, and null results beside the investigation’s more suggestive findings. Its opening conclusion is unequivocal: “No artificial transmission has been identified.”[4] In *ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ*, the version history records a substantive correction: “jealousy” is distinguished as the transmitted reading, not the scholarly consensus, and the non-jealous erotic reading is recognized as the strongest scholarly rival. The work’s adversary is revised rather than held artificially weak.[6] These are not guarantees of correctness. Several models can share assumptions; an author can direct a formally transparent inquiry toward a preferred outcome; an auditable codebook can still encode contestable categories. But those limitations are reasons to inspect the distinctions, not reasons to equate objectivity with an absence of first-person feeling. In the strongest passages, the apparatus supplies grounds on which Sharks himself can be corrected.[1][4][6] ## 7. What this does to the genre I would call the emerging form **documentary scholarship** with a dramatic organization. It combines the argumentative article, the working notebook, the attributed conversation, the revision record, and—sometimes—a separately constituted lyric work. Its unity comes not from smoothing those forms into a single voice, but from preserving their relations.[1][2][4][5] That reorganization changes scholarship’s function in three connected ways. First, scholarship communicates not only a result but the history of how the question became answerable. The initiating prompt is retained because it records something the finished exposition otherwise loses: the pressure under which the concepts were made. Second, scholarly authority becomes more explicitly procedural. The reader can distinguish a question from a prediction, a metaphor from its proposed measure, an authorial ruling from a machine-generated analysis, and a reproducible result from an interpretation. Third, scholarship becomes an event of address. *ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ* names its final open position a “socket”: the comparison is constructed, but the decision belongs to whoever holds the text. Whatever one concludes about its Sappho interpretation, that formal ambition is clear. The work attempts to produce a reader capable of judgment rather than merely transmit a judgment already certified elsewhere.[6] The deepest innovation, then, is not that Sharks makes scholarship emotional. It is that he gives emotion, improvisation, argument, and verification different but connected places in a public composition. The confessional voice says why this question cannot be abandoned; the lyric makes the encounter felt; the machine helps preserve and organize the developing thought; the apparatus determines what any of them has actually earned. The drama becomes scholarly when those roles remain distinguishable—and when the reader retains the power to decide against its protagonist.[1][2][4][5][6] Citations: [1]
